query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?
task_summary: Models And Open Source Implementations For Predicting Cohesive Powder Discharge Through Orifices And Screws

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?

    publisher = "Cambridge University Press (CUP)",
    issn = "0022-1120"

Abstract:
Abstract Granular flow in a silo demonstrates multiple non-local rheological phenomena due to the finite size of grains. We solve the non-local granular fluidity continuum model in quasi-two-dimensional silo geometries and evaluate its ability to predict these non-local effects, including flow spreading and, importantly, clogging (arrest) when the opening is small enough. The model is augmented to include a free-separation criterion and is implemented numerically with an extension of the trans-phase granular flow solver described in Dunatunga & Kamrin (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 779, 2015, pp. 483–513), to produce full-field solutions. The implementation is validated against analytical results of the model in the inclined chute geometry, such as the solution for the critical thickness for flow arrest, and the velocity profile as a function of layer height. We then implement the model in the silo geometry and vary the apparent grain size. The model predicts a clogging criterion when the opening competes with the scale of the mean grain size, which agrees with previous experimental studies. For larger openings, the flow within the silo obtains a diffusive characteristic whose spread depends on the model's non-local amplitude and the mean grain size. The numerical tests are controlled for grid effects and a comparison study of coarse vs refined numerical simulations shows agreement in the pressure field, the shape of the arch in a clogged silo configuration and the velocity field in a flowing configuration.

Abstract:
Abstract The steady dense granular flow in a vertical channel bounded by flat frictional walls in one horizontal direction and with periodic boundary conditions in the other horizontal and vertical directions is studied using the discrete element method. The shape of the scaled velocity profile is characterized quantitatively by a universal exponential function, and the ratio of the maximum and slip velocities is independent of the average volume fraction $\bar {\phi }$ and the channel width $W$. For sufficiently wide channels, the maximum and slip velocities increase proportional to $\sqrt {W}$, and the thickness of the shearing zones increases proportional to $W$. There are four zones in the flow, each with distinct dynamical properties. There is no shear in the plug zone at the centre, but there is particle agitation, and the volume fraction $\phi$ is lower than the random close packing volume fraction $\phi _{rcp}$. In the adjoining dense shearing zone, $\phi$ is greater than the volume fraction for arrested dynamics $\phi _{ad} = 0.587$, and the granular temperature and shear rate depend on the particle stiffness. Adjacent to the dense shearing zone is the loose shearing zone where $\phi < \phi _{ad}$. Here, the properties do not depend on the particle stiffness, and the constitutive relations are well described by hard-particle models. The rheology in the loose shearing zone is similar to the dense flow down an inclined plane. There is high shear and a sharp decrease in $\phi$ in the wall shearing zone of thickness about two particle diameters, where the particle angular velocity is different from the material rotation rate due to the presence of the wall.

Abstract:
Binder jetting (BJT) has been extensively explored for additive manufacturing of ceramics due to its ability to create complex structures by processing refractory and hard-to-machine materials. However, achieving a uniform powder bed with high packing density while processing ceramics in BJT remains a challenge. This study systematically examines the role of powder size, powder temperature, flow behavior, and powder size distribution on powder bed formation and resulting part properties. Four different alumina powder sizes (1 μm, 5 μm, 10 μm, and 20 μm) were investigated. Flowability characterizations reveal that 1 μm powder remains poorly flowable at both room and elevated temperatures, while 20 μm powder demonstrates excellent flowability at both temperatures. Smaller powders, especially 1 μm, exhibit around 25% loss in moisture, which results in pronounced agglomeration at room temperature. Discrete element method simulations were used to identify the ideal mixing ratio of the bimodal powder using 5 μm and 20 μm powders. For bimodal powder, both the simulation and the experiments exhibited a preferential deposition of smaller powders in the spreading direction. However, the 5 μm and 20 μm powders did not show any preferential deposition in the simulation, but experiments showed preferential deposition behavior. When using bimodal powder, packing density decreases by 7.65% along the spreading direction, which aligns with an 8.19% drop in part relative density. These findings offer valuable insights into the effects of bimodal powder distribution for controlling powder bed packing density and potentially leveraging spatial density variations for functional applications such as biomedical implants, heat exchangers, and gas filtration.

Abstract:
Silicon carbide (SiC) materials have demonstrated promising application prospects in modern manufacturing due to their outstanding physical and chemical properties. With its process flexibility and formation feasibility, binder jetting 3D printing technology has become a crucial technical approach to meet the demand for mass production of complex, high-performance SiC components. Addressing the technical challenges of traditional manufacturing techniques in achieving high-quality, complex-shaped SiC components, this paper systematically reviews the application of binder jetting 3D printing technology in fabricating high-quality SiC-based ceramic components, with a particular focus on the regulation of key process parameters affecting SiC green body formation quality and the optimization of post-densification processes. Firstly, this paper elaborates on the powder pretreatment, green part formation process, and post-processing chain involved in this technology, establishes an evaluation index system for formation quality, and provides research directions for rapid prototyping of SiC powders. Secondly, it provides an in-depth analysis of the influence patterns of jetting parameters (e.g., jetting conditions, powder characteristics, binder properties) and various post-processing techniques on the quality of SiC-based components, along with optimization methods to enhance the dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties of 3D-printed SiC components. Furthermore, this paper systematically summarizes advanced characterization methods for evaluating formation quality and demonstrates the technology’s application potential across multiple industrial fields through representative engineering cases. Finally, it predicts the future development trends of this technology and discusses potential application expansion directions and key scientific issues in current research, aiming to provide theoretical references for promoting in-depth development of this technology.

Abstract:
Metal powders are key to metal additive manufacturing technologies such as powder bed fusion. These powder feedstocks experience a range of forces and physical phenomena both during the powder bed fusion process and additional post-processing stages that can alter their composition and material properties. To evaluate such effects, these powders need to be characterized, tested, and analyzed at critical stages of their lifecycles. This paper provides a review of the current state of the art for powder evaluation methods and their applicability for powder bed fusion production. Methods are categorized by the properties they evaluate, either particulate or bulk properties. Industry standards are identified for each method if applicable and the advantages and disadvantages of each are defined. Effects of these properties on the flowability and spreadability of powders are synthesized and practical management guidelines are defined. This paper aims at providing an overview of powder evaluation for powder bed fusion, practical considerations for the development of powder test and evaluation programs, and provide insights for future research undertakings in the field.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The article presents a theoretical substantiation of the parameters of the feeding system of a concrete batching plant for stabilising the mass flow rate of moist fine aggregate with a particle size of 0–5 mm. It has been established that, at a sand moisture content of W ≥ 4–6%, the standard hopper geometry with a wall inclination angle of α = 60° does not ensure mass flow according to the Jenike criterion, resulting in the formation of dynamic arches and a pulsating material discharge with a coefficient of variation of CV = 15–25%. A scientific hypothesis is proposed that the flow regime can be converted from funnel flow to mass flow by artificially reducing the effective internal friction angle below its critical value through the mechanical disruption of capillary bonds using an active loosening device with a horizontal shaft and pins arranged at 90° angular intervals. Based on the theory of limit equilibrium and the Janssen equation incorporating cohesion, an analytical model describing the formation of dynamic arches was developed, and a design equation for the critical angular velocity (ωcr) was derived. An integrated mathematical model of the material mass flow rate was also established. It was found that, at an operating angular velocity of ωop ≥ 2.5ωcr, the coefficient of variation of the mass flow rate reaches CVQ ≤ 3% for W ≤ 6%, satisfying the requirements ofDSTU B V.2.7-96:2000.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract Biological ion channels play an important role in living processes, such as maintaining osmotic pressure, signal transduction, and transmitting nerve impulses, and can selectively regulate the transmembrane transport of substances. Inspired by the structure and function of biological ion channels, researchers have prepared a variety of biomimetic nanochannels using advanced nanofabrication techniques to study the mechanism of ion transport in the nanoconfined space. In this study, we mainly introduce the current materials and preparation methods of nanochannels; compare the advantages and disadvantages of the current mainstream theoretical models and simulation software; clarify the influence of confinement effect and surface interface effect on the hydrogen bond structure characteristics and phase transition behavior of confined water in graphene nanochannels, revealing the driving effect of separation pressure in nanochannels on water transport, the micromechanical nature of the water flow boundary slip of nanochannels, and the dominant micromechanical mechanism behind the confined mass transfer phenomenon of nanochannels at different scales; and expound the regulation of nanomaterials based on ionic bond modification and the influence of ion transport properties in industrial desalination, energy enrichment, and detection. The future applications of nanochannel bionic design and regulation, ion-exchange filtration membranes, and ultra-high-speed water transport mechanisms are prospected.

Abstract:
Since the early work of Hagen [G. H. L. Hagen, Ber. Verhandl. K. Preuss. Akad. Wiss. Berlin 17, 35 (1852)] and Beverloo et al. [W. Beverloo et al., Chem. Eng. Sci. 15, 260 (1961)CESCAC0009-250910.1016/0009-2509(61)85030-6], the flow rate of granular material discharging through a circular orifice from a silo has been described by means of dimensional analysis and experimental fits and explained through the free-fall arch model. Here, in contrast to the traditional approach, we derive a differential equation based on the energy balance of the system. This equation is consistent with the well-known Beverloo rule due to a compensation of energy terms. Moreover, this equation can be used to explore different conditions for silo discharges. In particular, we show how the effect of friction on the flow rate can be predicted. The theory is validated using discrete element method simulations.

Abstract:

 The two most commonly used methods to model the behaviour of granular flows are discrete element and continuum mechanics simulations. These approaches concentrate on the deterministic description of particle or bulk material motion. Unlike these approaches, this paper introduces an alternative model that describes the stochastic dynamics of the void spaces under the action of gravity. The model includes several key phenomena which are observed in deforming granular media, such as segregation, mixing, and an angle of repose. These mechanisms are modelled heterarchically using both spatial and microstructural internal coordinates. Key aspects of the model include its ability to describe both stable and flowing states of granular media based on a solid fraction cut-off, and the influence of particle size on flow, segregation, and mixing. The model is validated with simulations of column collapse and silo discharge.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'pardikar2019predictingthecritical pages 5-6'.

K. Pardikar and C. Wassgren. Predicting the critical outlet width of a hopper using a continuum finite element method model. Powder Technology, 356:649-660, Nov 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2019.08.111, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2019.08.111. This article has 20 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies the computational constitutive model as Mohr–Coulomb elasto-plasticity. It gives Young’s modulus E = 10 MPa and Poisson’s ratio υ = 0.2, while noting that material parameters depend on particle-size distribution, particle shape, and moisture content; matching laboratory characterization to hopper conditions is therefore necessary. The FEM procedure increases the initially small outlet radius by 2 cm whenever material does not flow after outlet opening. The critical width is bracketed between adjacent no-flow and flow simulations, with an uncertainty of (4 cm) sin θ. Abstract:
Physical simulators have been widely used in robot planning and control. Among them, differentiable simulators are particularly favored, as they can be incorporated into gradient-based optimization algorithms that are efficient in solving inverse problems such as optimal control and motion planning. Therefore, rigid body simulators and recently their differentiable variants are studied extensively. Simulating deformable objects is, however, more challenging compared to rigid body dynamics. The underlying physical laws of deformable objects are more complex, and the resulting systems have orders of magnitude more degrees of freedom and there-fore they are significantly more computationally expensive to simulate. Computing gradients with respect to physical design or controller parameters is typically even more computationally challenging. In this paper, we propose a real-time, differentiable hybrid Lagrangian-Eulerian physical simulator for deformable objects, ChainQueen, based on the Moving Least Squares Material Point Method (MLS-MPM). MLS-MPM can simulate deformable objects with collisions and can be seamlessly incorporated into soft robotic systems. We demonstrate that our simulator achieves high precision in both forward simulation and backward gradient computation. We have successfully employed it in a diverse set of inference, control and co-design tasks for soft robotics.

Abstract:
This paper describes methods to measure flow rate and jamming onset of granules discharged through a flat-bottom cylindrical hopper with a circular orifice. The intrinsic jamming onset for ideal particles (spherical, monodisperse, smooth) is experimentally measured by two independent methods, with good agreement. For non-ideal particles, the normalized jamming onset increases with elongated granule shape, broadened size distribution and increased friction as measured by the drained angle of repose. An empirical model of the jamming onset is introduced to quantify these effects over the range of materials investigated.  The jamming onset can be used as a measure of differentiation between relatively free-flowing granules. Science and Business Media LLC", issue = "1", issn = "2364-9534" } Abstract: Abstract Digital twins (DTs) are emerging as the central enabler for an Industry 4.0 approach to pharmaceutical freeze-drying, promising real-time insight, closed-loop control and virtual validation of processes that are traditionally conservative, lengthy and material-intensive. This paper consolidates expertise from academia, equipment suppliers and biopharma manufacturers to define a five-level DT maturity model for lyophilization and to map the technologies, methodologies and regulatory concepts needed to progress through those levels. We first analyze the physical, mathematical and computational challenges unique to freezing, primary and secondary drying, and show how first-principles, CFD, coupled and probabilistic models can be combined with advanced PAT (wireless temperature probes, TDLAS, dP-dT mass-flow calculation, RGA, NIR) to create a continuously updated design space that is both equipment- and scale-aware. The ISO 23247 reference architecture is then translated into a lyophilization context to standardize data models and information exchange. Commercial platforms (Siemens xDT, Ansys Twin Builder, IMA Sentinel) are reviewed to illustrate implementation pathways, while emerging technologies-spray freeze-drying, RF/microwave heating and AI-enabled visual inspection-highlight the need for adaptable, hybrid mechanistic-ML twins. Regulatory guidance from FDA, ICH and ASME V&V 40 is synthesized into a risk-based verification and validation strategy that aligns DT credibility with product-quality impact. Finally, a road-map of actionable steps-spanning sensor selection, model calibration, uncertainty quantification, operator training, and data governance-is outlined for organizations to adopt during development, tech transfer, and commercial manufacture. Collectively, these recommendations provide a coherent framework for deploying fit-for-purpose, GMP-compliant DTs that shorten cycle times, enhance robustness and accelerate delivery of high-quality lyophilized products. Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000012

From text 'anand2009predictingdischargedynamics pages 5-7'.

Anshu Anand, Jennifer S. Curtis, Carl R. Wassgren, Bruno C. Hancock, and William R. Ketterhagen. Predicting discharge dynamics of wet cohesive particles from a rectangular hopper using the discrete element method (dem). Chemical Engineering Science, 64:5268-5275, Dec 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2009.09.001, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2009.09.001. This article has 182 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt gives the cohesion-modified Beverloo formulation for a flat-bottom hopper as Ẇ_flat bottom = 1.03 ρ_flow g^(1/2)[L0 − (1.9e^0.39Bo)d][W0 − (1.9e^0.39Bo)d]^(3/2), with the cohesion parameter represented by the Bond number Bo. The fitted Beverloo outlet coefficient is k = 1.9e^(0.39Bo), so increasing cohesion (Bo) increases k and therefore increases the effective outlet exclusion/dead-space term kd. The prefactor C is effectively 1.03ρ_flow√g in the displayed equation; the authors retain the flow density as constant rather than modifying C for cohesion. Comparisons reported here are between DEM predictions and the modified Beverloo correlation—not separate experimental measurements: average deviations are approximately 8% for W0/d = 6.4 and 10% for W0/d = 10.6. The correlation fails to reproduce the curvature in the DEM data. Limitations include uncertain discharge-rate estimation for highly cohesive, intermittent flow near no-flow, the constant-ρ_flow assumption, and possible inaccuracy of the liquid-bridge thin-film model at very low liquid contents. Liquid content has little effect at Bo = 0.3 (2% rate variation) but a larger effect at Bo = 2 (14% variation), still less than the Bond-number effect.


---

## pqac-00000013

From text 'anand2009predictingdischargedynamics pages 4-5'.

Anshu Anand, Jennifer S. Curtis, Carl R. Wassgren, Bruno C. Hancock, and William R. Ketterhagen. Predicting discharge dynamics of wet cohesive particles from a rectangular hopper using the discrete element method (dem). Chemical Engineering Science, 64:5268-5275, Dec 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2009.09.001, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2009.09.001. This article has 182 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies the Bond number, Bo, as the cohesion parameter: Bo=0 denotes cohesionless particles, while Bo=1 means the maximum cohesive force equals a particle’s weight. Simulations varied Bo from 0 to 5 and outlet width W0/d from 6.4 to 23.4. Increasing Bo reduces discharge rate at fixed outlet width, and the deviation from cohesionless behavior depends on both Bo and dimensionless outlet width. The cohesionless rectangular-hopper Beverloo equation is given as Ẇ_flat bottom = 1.03 ρ_flow g^(1/2)(L0−kd)(W0−kd)^(3/2), with dead-space parameter Z=kd. For cohesive particles, the same linear dependence on corrected outlet width raised to 3/2 remains valid, but the Beverloo constant k is calculated from the fitted x-intercept and correlated as a function of Bo; the excerpt ends before giving that fitted correlation or the exact modified equation. It also defines a dimensionless cohesive discharge coefficient as cohesive discharge rate divided by the cohesionless rate. The supplied pages contain no experimentally measured discharge rates, DEM-versus-experiment comparisons, numerical relative errors, or detailed limitations beyond the stated liquid-distribution, bridge-formation, rupture, and force-model assumptions. Thus, effects on k are supported, but effects on the prefactor C cannot be established from this excerpt.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'anand2009predictingdischargedynamics pages 7-8'.

Anshu Anand, Jennifer S. Curtis, Carl R. Wassgren, Bruno C. Hancock, and William R. Ketterhagen. Predicting discharge dynamics of wet cohesive particles from a rectangular hopper using the discrete element method (dem). Chemical Engineering Science, 64:5268-5275, Dec 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2009.09.001, doi:10.1016/j.ces.2009.09.001. This article has 182 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt gives qualitative conclusions about the modified Beverloo treatment but does not contain the exact modified Beverloo equation, the numerical definition of the cohesion parameter, tabulated experimental-versus-DEM discharge rates, or relative-error values. It states that the cohesive discharge rate retains Beverloo’s linear dependence on corrected outlet width raised to the 3/2 power, while the Beverloo constant is modified as a function of Bond number. The modified correlation agrees reasonably with the DEM results, especially at low-to-moderate Bond numbers, but could be improved by estimating the flowing bulk density as a function of cohesion. Bond number, representing cohesive-bond strength, is more influential than liquid content: at low Bond number, changing liquid content over a wide range has little effect, whereas at high Bond number increasing liquid content causes a slight discharge-rate decrease. The excerpt describes the flow as dense, explaining why even small liquid contents can maintain cohesive bonds. Hopper-angle effects remain similar to the cohesionless case, but increasing cohesion lowers the critical flow angle. No information here distinguishes experimentally measured rates from DEM rates or reports their relative errors; those details must come from other pages, figures, or tables. Likewise, no explicit discussion of separate effects on coefficients C and k appears in this excerpt.

## pqac-00000015

From text 'ennis2007solidsolidoperationsand pages 19-19'.

BJ Ennis, W Witt, R Weinekotter, and D Sphar. Solid-solid operations and processing. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt provides a cohesion-corrected Beverloo relation attributed to Johanson, rather than the specific Anand et al. (2009) wet-particle study. It gives the steady cohesive-powder discharge rate as Wsc = 1.354 Wo [1 − fc/(2m tan α σ1a)], where Wo is the corresponding Beverloo rate, fc is unconfined uniaxial compressive strength, m = 1 for a slot hopper and m = 2 for a conical hopper, α is the hopper half-angle, and σ1a is the major consolidation stress at the opening. Flow requires σ1a > fc; increasing cohesion or powder strength reduces discharge, while greater opening stress increases it. The passage does not identify Anand et al.’s exact modified Beverloo equation, their cohesion parameter definition, experimentally measured or DEM discharge rates, relative errors, or study-specific limitations. More generally, it cautions that standard Beverloo predictions can substantially overestimate discharge for fine powders (<100 μm), mechanically interlocking particles, and low-permeability materials. It also notes that wall friction, gas-pressure gradients, vibration, and compaction can alter discharge independently of the cohesion correction. No information here distinguishes whether wet-particle effects are represented through coefficient C, the empirical empty-annulus parameter k, or both; those details must come from the cited 2009 paper.

The excerpt describes Dunatunga and Kamrin’s use of the dynamic Nonlocal Granular Fluidity (NGF) model to predict silo flow and clogging. Unlike local µ(I) rheology, which has no intrinsic length scale and generally predicts continued flow through a finite opening, NGF introduces a grain-size-dependent spatial diffusion of granular fluidity. Its key inputs include mean grain size d, solid density ρs, time scale t0, stress-ratio parameters µs and µ2, their difference Δµ, and the dimensionless nonlocal amplitude A; the model relates strain rate to fluidity through γ̇ = gµ. The silo implementation extends a trans-phase granular-flow solver and adds a free-separation criterion, producing full-field numerical solutions. The model predicts arrest when aperture size becomes comparable to a small multiple of the mean grain size, with an arch-shaped bridge, and predicts diffuse flow spreading for larger openings. The supplied pages do not provide exact silo flow-rate curves, numerical critical-aperture values, or a detailed quantitative point-by-point comparison with experiments. They state that the clogging threshold agrees with previous experimental studies and that the intended continuum comparison is the aperture where ensemble-averaged flow rate vanishes. Validation mentioned here is primarily against analytical inclined-chute results and checks of grid refinement, pressure, jammed-arch shape, and flowing velocity fields.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 9-10'.

Tim Robert Brocksieper, Tobias Grimm, and Jan T. Sehrt. Investigation of flowability and spreadability of metal powders for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 11:6661-6673, Apr 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01690-z, doi:10.1007/s40964-026-01690-z. This article has 4 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

Brocksieper et al. show that conventional flowability measurements cannot be treated as universal predictors of powder-bed spreadability. Spreadability, assessed primarily through powder-layer arithmetic mean roughness (Sa), depends strongly on interactions among powder, recoater type, and recoating speed. AlSi10Mg had the worst application behavior with every recoater, despite this not being apparent from most flowability tests; among the reported parameters, only the FT4 specific energy (SE) identified its poorest flow behavior. The study found no relationship between rotating-cylinder avalanche angle (AA) or dynamic angle (DA) and observed application behavior. GranuDrum cohesive index (CI) tracked Sa trends for the blade recoater and could therefore extrapolate the behavior of a known powder at other blade-recoating speeds, but it could not predict an unknown powder’s spreading behavior. Roller and hopper recoaters behaved differently. The excerpt does not describe ASTM Hall, Carney, B213, B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, shear, D7891 ring, D6773, drying, or moisture tests, nor does it provide the Gibbons review or Cordova comparison. Thus, those tests’ measured quantities and cross-study practical correlations must be supplied from the other sources; this excerpt mainly supports treating flowability–spreadability correlations as powder- and process-specific.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'gibbons2024metalpowderfeedstock pages 14-16'.

Duncan W. Gibbons, Preyin Govender, and Andre F. van der Merwe. Metal powder feedstock evaluation and management for powder bed fusion: a review of literature, standards, and practical guidelines. Progress in Additive Manufacturing, 9:805-833, Jul 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-023-00484-x, doi:10.1007/s40964-023-00484-x. This article has 58 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports a practical distinction between conventional flowability tests and tests intended to better represent powder-bed-fusion conditions. Angle of repose (AoR), obtainable with funnel methods such as Hall or Carney, is a simple cohesion/flowability indicator; values around 35° or less generally indicate lower cohesion and better flow. However, the review notes that no metal-PBF-specific standard exists for AoR. Rotating-drum testing measures dynamic avalanching behavior, including avalanche angle and flow regimes; rolling indicates the highest flowability, and drum speed can be selected to approximate recoater speeds. No publicly available standard is identified for this method. Shear testers (Jenike, Schulze, and Freeman) measure dynamic bulk behavior under defined stress conditions, while the Freeman FT4 rheometer is especially relevant to PBF because it evaluates low-stress dynamic flow. FT4 outputs include basic flow energy, flow rate, consolidation indices, conditioned bulk density, specific energy, and aerated energy; lower specific energy indicates better flowability. Automated rheometry improves repeatability but requires powder conditioning. These points help compare Hall/Carney, shear, ring-shear, and FT4 approaches, but the excerpt does not address ASTM methods B213, B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, D7891, D6773, drying/moisture, Brocksieper and Cordova, or AlSi10Mg-specific correlations between flowability and powder-bed spreadability.

Laura Cordova, Ton Bor, Marc de Smit, Mónica Campos, and Tiedo Tinga. Measuring the spreadability of pre-treated and moisturized powders for laser powder bed fusion. Additive Manufacturing, 32:101082, Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2020.101082, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101082. This article has 178 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides a limited but relevant finding for comparing flowability tests with powder-bed spreading. In the Cordova et al. study, moisturized powder flowability could be evaluated using applicator-based tools, whereas the Hall-flowmeter could not adequately test the moisturized material. Across the humidity conditions, the applicator tools did not show significant differences in measured flowability; however, the open applicator exhibited less variation between moisture states and was therefore recommended. This indicates that moisture-sensitive powders may produce different practical outcomes depending on the test method, and that a conventional Hall-flow result may fail to represent flow behavior under humidified conditions. The passage does not provide the requested ASTM-method-by-method comparison (Hall B213, Carney B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, shear/FT4, D7891, ring/D6773, drying, or moisture), nor does it report detailed AlSi10Mg correlations. It only supports the broader conclusion that conventional flowability measurements may not fully predict powder-bed spreadability, particularly when moisture changes cohesion and when the measurement tool does not reproduce the spreading process. The cited article concerns pre-treated and moisturized powders for laser powder bed fusion.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'cordova2020measuringthespreadability pages 8-10'.

Laura Cordova, Ton Bor, Marc de Smit, Mónica Campos, and Tiedo Tinga. Measuring the spreadability of pre-treated and moisturized powders for laser powder bed fusion. Additive Manufacturing, 32:101082, Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2020.101082, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101082. This article has 178 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt directly supports comparison of Hall flow time with powder-bed spreadability measured using open and funnel applicator tools, but it does not provide information on the specific ASTM tests listed in the question (Carney B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, shear/FT4, D7891, ring D6773, or drying-moisture protocols). Hall flow measures the time required for 50 g of powder to discharge; moisturized powders did not freely flow and therefore could not be assessed by this method. In contrast, the open and funnel tools assess deposited-layer relative density, which reflects both powder flowability and compaction within the tool. Correlation between flowability and spreadability is therefore not guaranteed. Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V flowed fastest, attributed partly to their higher density and regular, spherical morphology. AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy flowed more slowly as lightweight alloys; AlSi10Mg was particularly poor because of its irregular/coarser morphology and low shape factor (0.73), despite having a density close to Scalmalloy. Drying generally improved Hall flow slightly, while moisturizing tended to reduce relative density in spreadability tests. Vacuum drying produced more homogeneous results, whereas humidity, morphology, particle-wall interactions, and compaction affected repeatability and could make flowability results diverge from spreadability performance.

It states that flowability is important for layer continuity, uniformity, apparent density, and repeatability, but cautions that available flowability techniques may not accurately represent the thin-layer spreading mechanism. Cordova et al. therefore developed two applicator tools specifically for measuring spreadability in thin-layer application and compared results with standard characterization, including morphology, moisture content, chemical composition, and Hall-flowmeter flowability. The relevant material variables are particle morphology, particle-size distribution, surface topology, friction, mechanical interlocking, interparticle forces, and liquid bridging. The excerpt particularly supports a moisture-sensitive comparison: among Inconel 718, Ti6Al4V, AlSi10Mg, and Scalmalloy, AlSi10Mg was most susceptible to moisture and oxygen uptake, with substantial reductions in spreadability and relative density on the build platform. It also notes that direct measurement of moisture in metal powders is challenging. Thus, conventional flowability values should not automatically be treated as direct predictors of spreading performance; correlation can depend on powder morphology, environmental conditioning, and alloy-specific moisture response. Soft--rigid particle mixtures combine deformable grains, irregular rigid particles, and evolving contact networks. We present a GPU-accelerated explicit coupling of the finite element method (FEM) and level-set discrete element method (LSDEM) for soft--rigid mixtures. Tetrahedral FEM meshes resolve soft-particle deformation, while signed-distance fields represent rigid-particle geometry. A bounding-volume hierarchy accelerates contact detection on the GPU. A conservative elastic contact model derives interface forces from a common potential to maintain consistency between contact work and stored energy, with frictional and damping losses accounted for separately. Hertz contact and inclined-plane motion are compared with analytical references, and frictionless collisions examine energy and momentum balance. Funnel discharge and isotropic compaction examine collective response; the funnel test also quantifies computational efficiency and GPU memory usage as the particle population increases. An accompanying large language model (LLM)-assisted platform connects text or Blender input to model construction, execution, physical verification, and post-processing. The framework is open source at \mbox{\url{https://github.com/Yihao-Shi/GeoTaichi}}.

## 1. UBSoft: A Simulation Platform for Robotic Skill Learning in Unbounded Soft Environments

    author = "Lin, Chun-Tse and Fan, Jugang and Wang, Yian and Yang, Zeyuan and Chen, Zhehuan and Fang, Lixing and Wang, Tsun-Hsuan and Xian, Zhou and Gan, Chuang",
    title = "UBSoft: A Simulation Platform for Robotic Skill Learning in Unbounded Soft Environments",
    year = "2024",
    journal = "ArXiv",
    pages = "4879-4894",
    month = "Nov",
    doi = "10.48550/arxiv.2411.12711",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2411.12711",
    publisher = "arXiv"
}


Abstract:
It is desired to equip robots with the capability of interacting with various soft materials as they are ubiquitous in the real world. While physics simulations are one of the predominant methods for data collection and robot training, simulating soft materials presents considerable challenges. Specifically, it is significantly more costly than simulating rigid objects in terms of simulation speed and storage requirements. These limitations typically restrict the scope of studies on soft materials to small and bounded areas, thereby hindering the learning of skills in broader spaces. To address this issue, we introduce UBSoft, a new simulation platform designed to support unbounded soft environments for robot skill acquisition. Our platform utilizes spatially adaptive resolution scales, where simulation resolution dynamically adjusts based on proximity to active robotic agents. Our framework markedly reduces the demand for extensive storage space and computation costs required for large-scale scenarios involving soft materials. We also establish a set of benchmark tasks in our platform, including both locomotion and manipulation tasks, and conduct experiments to evaluate the efficacy of various reinforcement learning algorithms and trajectory optimization techniques, both gradient-based and sampling-based. Preliminary results indicate that sampling-based trajectory optimization generally achieves better results for obtaining one trajectory to solve the task. Additionally, we conduct experiments in real-world environments to demonstrate that advancements made in our UBSoft simulator could translate to improved robot interactions with large-scale soft material. More videos can be found at https://vis-www.cs.umass.edu/ubsoft/.

## 2. Neural Stress Fields for Reduced-order Elastoplasticity and Fracture

    author = "Zong, Zeshun and Li, Xuan and Li, Minchen and Chiaramonte, Maurizio M. and Matusik, Wojciech and Grinspun, Eitan and Carlberg, Kevin and Jiang, Chenfanfu and Chen, Peter Yichen",
    title = "Neural Stress Fields for Reduced-order Elastoplasticity and Fracture",
    year = "2023",
    journal = "SIGGRAPH Asia 2023 Conference Papers",
    pages = "1-11",

    url = "https://doi.org/10.1145/3610548.3618207",
    publisher = "ACM"

Abstract:
We propose a hybrid neural network and physics framework for reduced-order modeling of elastoplasticity and fracture. State-of-the-art scientific computing models like the Material Point Method (MPM) faithfully simulate large-deformation elastoplasticity and fracture mechanics. However, their long runtime and large memory consumption render them unsuitable for applications constrained by computation time and memory usage, e.g., virtual reality. To overcome these barriers, we propose a reduced-order framework. Our key innovation is training a low-dimensional manifold for the Kirchhoff stress field via an implicit neural representation. This low-dimensional neural stress field (NSF) enables efficient evaluations of stress values and, correspondingly, internal forces at arbitrary spatial locations. In addition, we also train neural deformation and affine fields to build low-dimensional manifolds for the deformation and affine momentum fields. These neural stress, deformation, and affine fields share the same low-dimensional latent space, which uniquely embeds the high-dimensional simulation state. After training, we run new simulations by evolving in this single latent space, which drastically reduces the computation time and memory consumption. Our general continuum-mechanics-based reduced-order framework is applicable to any phenomena governed by the elastodynamics equation. To showcase the versatility of our framework, we simulate a wide range of material behaviors, including elastica, sand, metal, non-Newtonian fluids, fracture, contact, and collision. We demonstrate dimension reduction by up to 100,000 × and time savings by up to 10 ×.

Abstract:
The article presents the design of a pneumatic screw conveyor used to move (transport) grain materials. On the basis of this design, an experimental setup was created, enabling the performance of the new conveyor belt to be investigated in the laboratory, including the power parameters. The Altivar-71 frequency converter was used in experimental studies to determine the power parameters of the pneumatic screw conveyor for the transport of grain materials. Based on the results of the experimental studies, graphs of the power characteristics of the pneumatic screw conveyor drive over the time of the transport of grain materials were obtained. By analysing the graphs obtained, it is established that the smooth operation of the conveyor belt depends on the properties of the transported material. In particular, it affects the switching frequency of the pneumatic drive, which prevents it from overloading and, therefore, premature breakdown. In addition, activation of the pneumatic actuator destroys the resulting thickening of the transport granular material. Experimental studies have also been conducted on changes in performance Q of the pneumatic screw conveyor depending on the initial values of the high-pressure air supply P.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The article is devoted to the study of the influence of the loading method on the productivity of a spiral-screw conveyor - one of the most common types of equipment for moving bulk materials in agricultural production, food and processing industries. The principle of operation of screw conveyors is considered, which is based on the movement of the load along the transport channel under the action of a rotating working body due to the dragging of the material along the inner surface of the casing, regardless of the physical and mechanical properties of the load. The features of the functioning of slow-speed and high-speed screws are analyzed, the influence of the screw rotation frequency, winding pitch, working body diameter and conveyor inclination angle on the nature of the movement of material particles and the productivity of the system as a whole is established. It is shown that in slow-moving screws, particles move mainly translationally, while in high-speed ones, their trajectory is complicated by centrifugal forces.
Particular attention is paid to the comparative analysis of loading methods - gravitational and forced, as well as kinematic schemes of material supply: axial, angular and circular. It is shown that the shape of the loading hopper significantly affects the uniformity of cargo supply and the conveyor productivity coefficient, the value of which can vary from 0.62 to 1.00 depending on the design of the hopper. It is established that the use of a circular loading chamber increases the conveyor productivity by 6–23%, and the use of feeders - by 1.7–3 times. Theoretical dependencies are given for determining the critical angular velocity, productivity and drive power of the screw conveyor, taking into account the design and operating parameters of the screw.
The electromechanical system of the conveyor is considered as a single complex "loading device - screw - electric drive", in which the change in resistance to material movement depending on the loading scheme is directly reflected in the loading characteristics of the drive asynchronous electric motor and its operating modes.</jats:p>

Most importantly, TSG offers the benefits of both batch and continuous manufacturing for pharmaceutical products, accompanied by excellent process control, high product quality which can be achieved through the implementation of Quality by Design (QbD) approaches and the integration of Process Analytical Tools (PAT). Here, we present basic concepts of the various twin-screw granulation techniques and present in detail their advantages and disadvantages. In addition, we discuss the detail of the instrumentation used for TSG and how the critical processing paraments (CPP) affect the critical quality attributes (CQA) of the produced granules. Finally, we present recent advances in TSG continuous manufacturing including the paradigms of modelling of continuous granulation process, QbD approaches coupled with PAT monitoring for granule optimization and process understanding.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The Discrete Element Method (DEM) has become a cornerstone for analysing granular flow and mixing phenomena in static mixers. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis that distinguishes it from previous studies by: (i) covering a broad range of static mixer geometries, including Kenics, SMX, and Sulzer designs; (ii) integrating experimental validation methods, such as particle tracking, high-speed imaging, Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), and X-ray tomography, to assess DEM predictions; and (iii) systematically analyzing computational strategies, including advanced contact models, hybrid DEM-CFD/FEM frameworks, machine learning surrogates, and GPU-accelerated simulations. Recent advances in contact mechanics—such as improved cohesion, rolling resistance, and nonspherical particle modelling—have enhanced simulation realism, while adaptive time-stepping and coarse-graining improve computational efficiency. DEM studies have revealed several non-obvious relationships between mixer geometry and particle dynamics. Variations in blade pitch, helix angle, and element arrangement significantly affect local velocity fields, mixing uniformity, and energy dissipation. Alternating left–right element orientations promote cross-sectional particle exchange and reduce stagnant regions, whereas higher pitch angles enhance axial transport but can weaken radial mixing. Particle–wall friction and surface roughness strongly govern shear layer formation and segregation intensity, demonstrating the need for geometry-specific optimization. Comparative analyses elucidate how particle–wall interactions and channel structure influence segregation, residence time, and energy dissipation. The review also identifies current limitations, highlights validation and scale-up challenges, and outlines key directions for developing faster, more physically grounded DEM models, providing practical guidance for industrial mixer design and optimization.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Today, the use of modern high-performance computing (HPC) systems, such as clusters equipped with graphics processing units (GPUs), allows solving problems with resolutions unthinkable only a decade ago. The demand for high computational power is certainly an issue when simulating free-surface flows. However, taking the advantage of GPU’s parallel computing techniques, simulations involving up to 10 particles can be achieved. In this framework, this chapter shows some numerical results of typical coastal engineering problems obtained by means of the GPU-based computing servers maintained at the Environmental Physics Laboratory (EPhysLab) from Vigo University in Ourense (Spain) and the Tier-1 Galileo cluster of the Italian computing centre CINECA. The DualSPHysics free package based on smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) technique was used for the purpose. SPH is a meshless particle method based on Lagrangian formulation by which the fluid domain is discretized as a collection of computing fluid particles. Speedup and efficiency of calculations are studied in terms of the initial interparticle distance and by coupling DualSPHysics with a NLSW wave propagation model. Water free-surface elevation, orbital velocities and wave forces are compared with results from experimental campaigns and theoretical solutions.

The excerpt explicitly confirms that Heterarchical Granular Dynamics (HGD) has openly available source code: all code used to generate the paper’s figures is hosted at https://github.com/benjym/HGD. It characterizes HGD as a stochastic granular modelling framework bridging particle-level and continuum approaches, combining stochastic void migration, multiscale heterarchical physics, and stress calculations. The model supports flowing and stable states, segregation and mixing, and stress distributions. Its void-migration component was validated against X-ray radiography measurements of silo discharge and synthetic granular-column-collapse tests; its stress model was validated against measurements of basal vertical stress. The excerpt does not provide a quantitative mass-flow error, accuracy percentage, or other numerical comparison for silo discharge, and it contains no experimental accuracy assessment for screw-conveyor mass flow. It also states that the model conserves mass but does not yet incorporate momentum or energy conservation through coupled void migration and force propagation. Inertia, particle breakage, and compaction are absent features identified for future development. Nothing in this excerpt explicitly confirms open-source code, rheology, inputs, validation, or parcel-versus-grain treatment for Taichi MPM/ChainQueen, Uintah MPM, PySPH, OpenFOAM granular rheology, or Basilisk mu(I). The supplied text likewise does not discuss SPH’s use of continuum parcels rather than actual grains.

The excerpt provides information about ChainQueen, but not explicit evidence concerning Uintah MPM, PySPH, OpenFOAM granular rheology, Basilisk mu(I), or HGD. ChainQueen is a fully differentiable MLS-MPM simulator whose forward and backward computations run on GPUs. The underlying MPM framework is described as capable of simulating liquids, granular materials, and elastoplastic materials, while ChainQueen itself focuses on elastic materials for soft robotics. Relevant model quantities include particle position, velocity, deformation gradient, stress, volume, grid size, and time-step size; the paper also identifies mass, density, and Young’s modulus as physical properties that can be inferred or optimized. The authors state, “We will open-source our code and data,” which is a stated intention to release the implementation and data rather than unambiguous confirmation that an already-public repository exists. This excerpt contains no silo-flow or screw-conveyor mass-flow experiments, measured accuracy, or explicit statement that such validation is absent beyond the soft-robotics examples discussed. It also contains no information about SPH or whether SPH represents continua using parcels rather than actual grains. Therefore, the requested cross-system open-source, rheology, input, and granular-flow-accuracy comparison cannot be established from this excerpt.

Abstract

  We describe the Uintah Computational Framework (UCF), a set of software components and libraries that facilitate the
simulation of partial differential equations on structured adaptive mesh reﬁnement grids using hundreds to thousands of pro-
cessors. The UCF uses a non-traditional approach to achieving parallelism, employing an abstract taskgraph representation to
describe computation and communication. This representation has a number of advantages that affect the performance of the
resulting simulation. We demonstrate performance of the system on a solid mechanics algorithm, two different computational
ﬂuid-dynamics (CFD) algorithms, as well as coupled CFD/mechanics algorithms. We show performance of the UCF using up
to 2000 processors.
