{"answer": "# Granular-discharge models for a small cohesive-powder auger

**Recommendation.** Use a calibrated screw-capacity model for mean mass per revolution, coupled to a separate probabilistic outlet-arching, afterflow, and tapping model. Use the existing DEM selectively to constrain that model and investigate mechanisms. Shear-cell-based hopper design is valuable for screening blockage, and continuum simulations can test geometry changes, but none of the cited validations establishes an accurate, transferable prediction of *increment-by-increment* delivery from a tapped, approximately 3-mm outlet at 1–30 rpm. In particular, matching salt at 105 mg/revolution at one operating point does not identify the contact parameters of the other powders. Published percentage errors below refer to their stated test geometries, not this doser. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000050)

## Model selection and quantitative evidence

| Model | Inputs and useful prediction | Validation and limitation for this doser |
|---|---|---|
| **Beverloo; cohesion-modified Beverloo** | For a freely draining circular aperture, \(\dot m=C\rho_b\sqrt g\,(D-kd)^{5/2}\): bulk density, aperture diameter, representative grain diameter, and fitted \(C,k\). A wedge/slot has a different geometric exponent. For wet spherical grains, Anand *et al.* fitted the effective-size coefficient \(k=1.9\exp(0.39Bo)\), where \(Bo\) is maximum cohesive force divided by grain weight; increasing cohesion reduces the effective opening. | Anand’s correlation differed by approximately **8% and 10% from the DEM results used to develop it** at two tested outlet-to-grain ratios; these are **not** independent experimental errors. Neither this fit nor ordinary Beverloo resolves motor-driven replenishment, stationary arches, tapping, or afterflow. Apply it only to the gravity-draining part of an *open* outlet, after checking \(D/d\) and flow regime. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000016) |
| **Jenike–Johanson arching and hopper design** | Measure the flow function—unconfined yield strength \(f_c\) versus major consolidation stress \(\sigma_1\)—together with wall friction, bulk density, and hopper geometry; compare material strength with the stress available to break an arch to estimate a critical opening. A Johanson cohesion correction to an otherwise free-flowing discharge rate has been reported, but it still needs the stress at the opening. | Best used to classify blockage risk and guide outlet redesign, **not** as a guaranteed mass-per-revolution law. Low-stress flow functions can be curved: extrapolating a high-consolidation shear test toward the weakly consolidated outlet may give a substantially wrong critical width. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056) |
| **Janssen stress saturation** | From reservoir width, fill height, bulk density, lateral-stress ratio, and powder–wall friction, estimate how wall support makes vertical stress saturate with depth. Feed the resulting stress estimate into an arch or consolidation calculation. | A *stress closure*, not a discharge-rate prediction. Reservoir depletion, wall material, and tapping can change its assumptions; do not substitute hydrostatic head for measured low-stress strength. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052) |
| **Screw-conveyor volumetric efficiency; Roberts-type design approaches** | Start with displaced volume per turn, approximately \(V_p=\pi p(D_s^2-D_h^2)/4\) for pitch \(p\), screw diameter \(D_s\), and hub diameter \(D_h\). Then \(m_{\rm rev}\simeq\rho_{b,\mathrm{channel}}V_p\eta\), with *effective* fill/transport efficiency \(\eta\) depending on tilt, speed, clearance, wall friction, pitch, feed availability, and backflow. This capacity must still be coupled to outlet release. | In a much larger screw-conveyor study, transport efficiencies varied substantially with pitch and speed; published experimental trends were compared with DEM, but the cited study does **not** supply a transferable percentage error for a 3-mm outlet. Its simulations were horizontal, largely used spherical particles, and did not establish performance for intermittent microdosing. Owen–Cleary-type DEM studies inform the dependence on screw geometry rather than providing an independently validated universal efficiency for these powders. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000029) |
| **Local \(\mu(I)\); nonlocal granular fluidity** | Local friction depends on inertial number, commonly \(I=d\dot\gamma/\sqrt{P/\rho_s}\); it needs particle size, solid density, pressure, and calibrated friction parameters. Nonlocal models additionally evolve a fluidity field and require a grain-scale cooperativity parameter, boundary conditions, and an arrest/free-separation rule. | Local rheology has difficulty predicting a grain-size-controlled finite-opening arrest. A **two-dimensional, cohesionless** nonlocal MPM study predicted the flow/no-flow transition between \(W/d=1\) and 1.5 for one parameter choice and compared it with previously measured thresholds around 1–1.16; it did **not** validate cohesive auger throughput. At a 3-mm outlet, a continuum approximation also becomes questionable if only a few grains or agglomerates span the opening. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) |
| **Mohr–Coulomb or Drucker–Prager FEM; MPM** | Represent yield, friction, cohesion, sometimes a compaction cap or stress-dependent flow function; supply density, elastic properties, internal and wall friction, strength versus consolidation, initial packing/stress, contact, and moving-boundary conditions. FEM is useful for a critical opening; MPM accommodates large deformation and separation more naturally. | In a wedge-hopper **critical-width**, not throughput, comparison, Mohr–Coulomb FEM bracketed **18.0–18.5 cm** against **20 cm** measured for polymer, and **8.8–9.4 cm** against **5 cm** for SiC. An assumed low-stress bilinear SiC flow function improved its predicted bracket to **5.5–6.1 cm**. These results show both the value of continuum mechanics and its sensitivity to low-stress characterization; they do not establish mg/revolution accuracy. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000050) |
| **SPH; stochastic cellular/avalanche models** | SPH discretizes a *continuum* into numerical parcels, requiring a chosen granular or yield-stress constitutive law, density/pressure and viscosity or plasticity closures, and wall/contact treatment; its numerical particles are not automatically physical powder grains. Stochastic void-migration/avalanche schemes instead need grain-size and packing descriptions, repose/stability criteria, and calibrated transition or migration rates. | Useful for free surfaces, intermittent-state surrogates, or rapid screening, but a fluid-style SPH calculation without a granular constitutive law cannot predict arching. The open HGD void-migration model reproduces selected silo **velocity-field** features against X-ray measurements of rice; its paper does not establish an error for mass flow through a cohesive auger and identifies missing momentum/energy coupling and compaction physics. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000051) |

**Code availability is distinct from validated capability.** The HGD authors provide figure-generating source code at `github.com/benjym/HGD`; PySPH is documented as open-source SPH software. Published work also establishes Uintah as an MPM framework and Taichi-based differentiable MPM implementations, including granular Drucker–Prager examples. OpenFOAM granular/continuum solvers and Basilisk are plausible development platforms, but the evidence assembled here does **not** verify a maintained, turnkey cohesive-screw implementation or a measured 3-mm auger mass-flow error for either. The cited critical-width FEM study used **Abaqus**, not an open-source solver; implementing its constitutive and opening procedure in an open FEM code would require independent verification. The nonlocal silo example used a research MPM implementation, not a demonstrated drop-in auger package. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053)

## Calibration and independent tests

1. **Separate transport from release.** Fit a measured channel-capacity term \(\rho_bV_p\eta(\theta,n,h,\mathrm{RH})\) and an outlet-state model. Give each commanded increment an open/blocked state; model flowing increment masses conditionally on that state, a separate tap-triggered release distribution, and a post-stop tail (the observed afterflow time constant). Include fill level, direction of tilt relative to gravity, print material and roughness, humidity, and tap protocol as recorded covariates. A mean-flow-only fit will otherwise mistake blocked increments and their subsequent release for changes in bulk friction. This is a proposed *fit-for-purpose model*, not a published prediction of the doser’s accuracy. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000050)

2. **Constrain rather than presume DEM parameters.** Supply measured size distribution and morphology, particle and loose/tapped bulk densities, and wall-contact measurements as inputs or informative priors. Infer a small number of identifiable *effective* quantities—such as cohesion relative to weight, particle/printed-wall friction, rolling resistance, and packing response—using the joint likelihood of mass/revolution, zero-flow frequency, tap mass, and afterflow. Treat humidity-dependent adhesion, batch variability, and simulator discrepancy explicitly. Agreement on one salt rate is a useful forward-model check, not proof that SJKR adhesion, contact friction, or rolling friction has been uniquely recovered. Test posterior predictions on powder, humidity, tilt, speed, and reservoir levels withheld from calibration. Low-stress shear data are especially valuable given the SiC hopper sensitivity to extrapolated strength. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057)

3. **Budget simulation strategically.** At the stated **26–30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution**, 100 one-revolution runs cost approximately **43–50 CPU-hours**, before equilibration, replication, or longer afterflow runs. Use replicated physical fingerprints and a space-filling subset of DEM cases to train an uncertainty-aware surrogate; add simulations where candidate parameter sets predict distinguishable fingerprints or where model uncertainty is high. Use posterior predictive checks rather than quoting a point-fit error as forecast accuracy. Differentiable MPM is not automatically an easy substitute: a Taichi-based granular parameter-identification benchmark reported that long, contact-rich GPU rollouts could even change a gradient’s sign with accumulation order. (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054)

4. **Use the tests for different questions.** ASTM **D7891** FT4 shear-cell and **D6773** Schulze ring-shear measurements constrain yield, internal friction, and flow function at *reported consolidation stresses*; measure the printed PLA/PETG wall-friction condition separately. **B213** Hall and **B964** Carney measure standardized funnel flow, with a *no-flow* result retained rather than converted to an arbitrary rate. **B212** apparent and **B527** tap density constrain packing and its sensitivity to agitation; **B214** sieving and **B822** laser diffraction constrain size distributions, supplemented by imaging for irregular shape; controlled loss-on-drying/conditioning tests characterize moisture sensitivity, not particle cohesion directly. Specify the moisture-conditioning and sample-handling history for every comparison. Hall and Carney no-flow results can be poorly repeatable for cohesive powders; shear strength and its low-consolidation curvature are more informative for arching than a single flow time. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058)

## Transfer to powder-bed spreadability

Treat the dosing fingerprint as a **candidate covariate**, not a substitute for a recoating test. Measure deposited-layer density or coverage, roughness, streaks/voids, and—where relevant—segregation under the actual blade, roller, or other recoater, layer thickness, and speed. In a metal-powder comparison including AlSi10Mg, the relationships between conventional flow indices and layer roughness changed with powder, recoater, and speed; a rotating-drum cohesive index tracked trends for a *known* powder with a blade but did not predict an unknown powder’s spreadability. Another study found that moisturized powders could fail the Hall test while still being characterized by powder-layer applicators, and reported marked AlSi10Mg sensitivity to moisture and oxygen uptake. Thus, evaluate whether the inferred cohesion/packing posteriors improve prediction of **held-out** layer outcomes beyond size, shape, density, and humidity alone. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037)"}

state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?

Reservoir depletion, wall material, and tapping can change its assumptions; do not substitute hydrostatic head for measured low-stress strength. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052) |
| **Screw-conveyor volumetric efficiency; Roberts-type design approaches** | Start with displaced volume per turn, approximately \(V_p=\pi p(D_s^2-D_h^2)/4\) for pitch \(p\), screw diameter \(D_s\), and hub diameter \(D_h\). Then \(m_{\rm rev}\simeq\rho_{b,\mathrm{channel}}V_p\eta\), with *effective* fill/transport efficiency \(\eta\) depending on tilt, speed, clearance, wall friction, pitch, feed availability, and backflow. This capacity must still be coupled to outlet release. | In a much larger screw-conveyor study, transport efficiencies varied substantially with pitch and speed; published experimental trends were compared with DEM, but the cited study does **not** supply a transferable percentage error for a 3-mm outlet. Its simulations were horizontal, largely used spherical particles, and did not establish performance for intermittent microdosing. Owen–Cleary-type DEM studies inform the dependence on screw geometry rather than providing an independently validated universal efficiency for these powders. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000029) |
| **Local \(\mu(I)\); nonlocal granular fluidity** | Local friction depends on inertial number, commonly \(I=d\dot\gamma/\sqrt{P/\rho_s}\); it needs particle size, solid density, pressure, and calibrated friction parameters. Nonlocal models additionally evolve a fluidity field and require a grain-scale cooperativity parameter, boundary conditions, and an arrest/free-separation rule. | Local rheology has difficulty predicting a grain-size-controlled finite-opening arrest. A **two-dimensional, cohesionless** nonlocal MPM study predicted the flow/no-flow transition between \(W/d=1\) and 1.5 for one parameter choice and compared it with previously measured thresholds around 1–1.16; it did **not** validate cohesive auger throughput. At a 3-mm outlet, a continuum approximation also becomes questionable if only a few grains or agglomerates span the opening. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) |
| **Mohr–Coulomb or Drucker–Prager FEM; MPM** | Represent yield, friction, cohesion, sometimes a compaction cap or stress-dependent flow function; supply density, elastic properties, internal and wall friction, strength versus consolidation, initial packing/stress, contact, and moving-boundary conditions. FEM is useful for a critical opening; MPM accommodates large deformation and separation more naturally. | In a wedge-hopper **critical-width**, not throughput, comparison, Mohr–Coulomb FEM bracketed **18.0–18.5 cm** against **20 cm** measured for polymer, and **8.8–9.4 cm** against **5 cm** for SiC. An assumed low-stress bilinear SiC flow function improved its predicted bracket to **5.5–6.1 cm**. These results show both the value of continuum mechanics and its sensitivity to low-stress characterization; they do not establish mg/revolution accuracy. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000050) |
| **SPH; stochastic cellular/avalanche models** | SPH discretizes a *continuum* into numerical parcels, requiring a chosen granular or yield-stress constitutive law, density/pressure and viscosity or plasticity closures, and wall/contact treatment; its numerical particles are not automatically physical powder grains. Stochastic void-migration/avalanche schemes instead need grain-size and packing descriptions, repose/stability criteria, and calibrated transition or migration rates. | Useful for free surfaces, intermittent-state surrogates, or rapid screening, but a fluid-style SPH calculation without a granular constitutive law cannot predict arching. The open HGD void-migration model reproduces selected silo **velocity-field** features against X-ray measurements of rice; its paper does not establish an error for mass flow through a cohesive auger and identifies missing momentum/energy coupling and compaction physics. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000051) |

**Code availability is distinct from validated capability.** The HGD authors provide figure-generating source code at `github.com/benjym/HGD`; PySPH is documented as open-source SPH software. Published work also establishes Uintah as an MPM framework and Taichi-based differentiable MPM implementations, including granular Drucker–Prager examples. OpenFOAM granular/continuum solvers and Basilisk are plausible development platforms, but the evidence assembled here does **not** verify a maintained, turnkey cohesive-screw implementation or a measured 3-mm auger mass-flow error for either. The cited critical-width FEM study used **Abaqus**, not an open-source solver; implementing its constitutive and opening procedure in an open FEM code would require independent verification. The nonlocal silo example used a research MPM implementation, not a demonstrated drop-in auger package. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053)

## Calibration and independent tests

1. **Separate transport from release.** Fit a measured channel-capacity term \(\rho_bV_p\eta(\theta,n,h,\mathrm{RH})\) and an outlet-state model. Give each commanded increment an open/blocked state; model flowing increment masses conditionally on that state, a separate tap-triggered release distribution, and a post-stop tail (the observed afterflow time constant). Include fill level, direction of tilt relative to gravity, print material and roughness, humidity, and tap protocol as recorded covariates. A mean-flow-only fit will otherwise mistake blocked increments and their subsequent release for changes in bulk friction. This is a proposed *fit-for-purpose model*, not a published prediction of the doser’s accuracy. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000050)

2. **Constrain rather than presume DEM parameters.** Supply measured size distribution and morphology, particle and loose/tapped bulk densities, and wall-contact measurements as inputs or informative priors. Infer a small number of identifiable *effective* quantities—such as cohesion relative to weight, particle/printed-wall friction, rolling resistance, and packing response—using the joint likelihood of mass/revolution, zero-flow frequency, tap mass, and afterflow. Treat humidity-dependent adhesion, batch variability, and simulator discrepancy explicitly. Agreement on one salt rate is a useful forward-model check, not proof that SJKR adhesion, contact friction, or rolling friction has been uniquely recovered. Test posterior predictions on powder, humidity, tilt, speed, and reservoir levels withheld from calibration. Low-stress shear data are especially valuable given the SiC hopper sensitivity to extrapolated strength. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057)

3. **Budget simulation strategically.** At the stated **26–30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution**, 100 one-revolution runs cost approximately **43–50 CPU-hours**, before equilibration, replication, or longer afterflow runs. Use replicated physical fingerprints and a space-filling subset of DEM cases to train an uncertainty-aware surrogate; add simulations where candidate parameter sets predict distinguishable fingerprints or where model uncertainty is high. Use posterior predictive checks rather than quoting a point-fit error as forecast accuracy. Differentiable MPM is not automatically an easy substitute: a Taichi-based granular parameter-identification benchmark reported that long, contact-rich GPU rollouts could even change a gradient’s sign with accumulation order. (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054)

4. **Use the tests for different questions.** ASTM **D7891** FT4 shear-cell and **D6773** Schulze ring-shear measurements constrain yield, internal friction, and flow function at *reported consolidation stresses*; measure the printed PLA/PETG wall-friction condition separately. **B213** Hall and **B964** Carney measure standardized funnel flow, with a *no-flow* result retained rather than converted to an arbitrary rate. **B212** apparent and **B527** tap density constrain packing and its sensitivity to agitation; **B214** sieving and **B822** laser diffraction constrain size distributions, supplemented by imaging for irregular shape; controlled loss-on-drying/conditioning tests characterize moisture sensitivity, not particle cohesion directly. Specify the moisture-conditioning and sample-handling history for every comparison. Hall and Carney no-flow results can be poorly repeatable for cohesive powders; shear strength and its low-consolidation curvature are more informative for arching than a single flow time. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058)

## Transfer to powder-bed spreadability

Treat the dosing fingerprint as a **candidate covariate**, not a substitute for a recoating test. Measure deposited-layer density or coverage, roughness, streaks/voids, and—where relevant—segregation under the actual blade, roller, or other recoater, layer thickness, and speed. In a metal-powder comparison including AlSi10Mg, the relationships between conventional flow indices and layer roughness changed with powder, recoater, and speed; a rotating-drum cohesive index tracked trends for a *known* powder with a blade but did not predict an unknown powder’s spreadability. Another study found that moisturized powders could fail the Hall test while still being characterized by powder-layer applicators, and reported marked AlSi10Mg sensitivity to moisture and oxygen uptake. Thus, evaluate whether the inferred cohesion/packing posteriors improve prediction of **held-out** layer outcomes beyond size, shape, density, and humidity alone. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037)

contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative information primarily for empirical granular discharge correlations, especially Beverloo-type silo/orifice flow. The standard Beverloo relation is W = Cρ√g(Do − kd)^(5/2), where C depends on discharge conditions, ρ is bulk or soil mass density, g is gravitational acceleration, Do is outlet diameter, k is a shape or wall-effect coefficient, and d is particle diameter. The reported typical range is 1.3 < k < 2.9; k = 2.9 was found for sands, while 1.4 is commonly used. A commonly used circular-opening value is C = 0.58. The cited experiments used linseed, spinach, watercress, rapeseed, kale, swede, turnip, and sand fractions, with particle sizes of 0.045–0.30 cm, densities of 0.57–1.5 g/cc, and outlet diameters of 0.26–3.02 cm. Validation is described as good for large orifices, but Beverloo fails for Do/d < 80, where clogging can occur. The Janda/Mancok modification introduces an exponential correction and predicts zero flow when outlet size equals particle diameter: W = C''√gρ[1 − 1/2e^(−b(D−d))](D−d)^(n+1/2), with n = 1 for 2D and n = 2 for 3D. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the continuum finite-element results and their comparison with analytical critical-outlet-width theories. FEM predictions are generally closer to Enstad’s theory than Jenike’s. Jenike’s radial-stress approach agrees near the outlet for Case A but increasingly diverges toward the upper free surface because it neglects that surface. The effect is especially important for Case B, where low internal friction and frictionless walls make the predicted critical width strongly dependent on material height; as height decreases, the critical width increases. For no-inflow discharge, the authors recommend using the largest prediction over all material heights. In the reported comparison, McLean is the most conservative, followed by Enstad, Jenike, and FEM. FEM–Enstad differences are attributed to differing arch geometries, localized rather than fully distributed yielding, and nonconstant principal stresses along circular arcs. Increasing wall friction worsens agreement with Enstad’s assumptions, while using Enstad’s arch shape in FEM produces widths closer to Enstad’s prediction. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the constitutive law as Abaqus’s Mohr–Coulomb elastoplastic model. It notes that alternative laws could be used, including Drucker–Prager Cap, Cam Clay, and nonlocal hypoplastic or granular-rheology models, but Mohr–Coulomb was selected partly because Jenike and Enstad approaches use it. The computational procedure consists of three explicit dynamic steps: the outlet is initially closed while gravity is smoothly applied; the material is then allowed to slide a small distance along the hopper wall to establish a passive consolidation stress state; finally, the outlet plate contact is deactivated and flow or no-flow is observed. The model uses plane-strain CPE4R elements, a rigid hopper wall, and half-domain symmetry. Residual internal and wall friction angles are used, while dilation is neglected. The excerpt states that elastic modulus and Poisson’s ratio have little effect on critical width, and that the model gives good comparison with experiments. However, it warns that no fracture model is included, parameter dependence on plastic strain may be needed for active consolidation states, and the provided text does not give laboratory shear-input values or precise predicted and experimental critical widths. Their continuum FEM implementation uses a Lagrangian formulation in Abaqus/6.14–6, with a symmetric wedge-shaped hopper under a 2D plane-strain assumption. The analytical comparison uses the modified effective yield locus (modified EYL); unconsolidated yield strength is obtained by assuming passive stress consolidation. The FEM model imposes a circular arch profile centered at the hopper apex because the implementation does not allow continuum fracture or natural arch evolution. After outlet opening, extensive deformation near the outlet indicates flow, while small deformations indicate no flow. The excerpt does not report laboratory shear-test inputs, a full constitutive-law specification, or precise FEM-versus-experiment critical-width values. It gives analytical comparison examples: for Case B, Jenike and Enstad predict flow at a 60 cm outlet, whereas McLean predicts no flow; for a 30 cm outlet, Jenike and McLean predict no flow while Enstad predicts flow when material height exceeds about 1 m. Stated limitations include simplified geometry, constant material properties, omission of material above the outlet, the plane-strain restriction, and the prescribed arch shape. contexts.context: The excerpt provides a cohesion-corrected Beverloo relation attributed to Johanson, rather than the specific Anand et al. (2009) wet-particle study. It gives the steady cohesive-powder discharge rate as Wsc = 1.354 Wo [1 − fc/(2m tan α σ1a)], where Wo is the corresponding Beverloo rate, fc is unconfined uniaxial compressive strength, m = 1 for a slot hopper and m = 2 for a conical hopper, α is the hopper half-angle, and σ1a is the major consolidation stress at the opening. Flow requires σ1a > fc; increasing cohesion or powder strength reduces discharge, while greater opening stress increases it. The passage does not identify Anand et al.’s exact modified Beverloo equation, their cohesion parameter definition, experimentally measured or DEM discharge rates, relative errors, or study-specific limitations. More generally, it cautions that standard Beverloo predictions can substantially overestimate discharge for fine powders (<100 μm), mechanically interlocking particles, and low-permeability materials. It also notes that wall friction, gas-pressure gradients, vibration, and compaction can alter discharge independently of the cohesion correction. No information here distinguishes whether wet-particle effects are represented through coefficient C, the empirical empty-annulus parameter k, or both; those details must come from the cited 2009 paper.

contexts.context: The excerpt gives the cohesion-modified Beverloo formulation for a flat-bottom hopper as Ẇ_flat bottom = 1.03 ρ_flow g^(1/2)[L0 − (1.9e^0.39Bo)d][W0 − (1.9e^0.39Bo)d]^(3/2), with the cohesion parameter represented by the Bond number Bo. The fitted Beverloo outlet coefficient is k = 1.9e^(0.39Bo), so increasing cohesion (Bo) increases k and therefore increases the effective outlet exclusion/dead-space term kd. The prefactor C is effectively 1.03ρ_flow√g in the displayed equation; the authors retain the flow density as constant rather than modifying C for cohesion. Comparisons reported here are between DEM predictions and the modified Beverloo correlation—not separate experimental measurements: average deviations are approximately 8% for W0/d = 6.4 and 10% for W0/d = 10.6. The correlation fails to reproduce the curvature in the DEM data. Limitations include uncertain discharge-rate estimation for highly cohesive, intermittent flow near no-flow, the constant-ρ_flow assumption, and possible inaccuracy of the liquid-bridge thin-film model at very low liquid contents. Liquid content has little effect at Bo = 0.3 (2% rate variation) but a larger effect at Bo = 2 (14% variation), still less than the Bond-number effect.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides Aschenbrenner and Funke’s analytical throughput framework but does not include the requested Roberts–Willis formulation by name. Mass throughput is represented by D, with the slip-free, completely filled maximum given as Dmax = nγV, where n is rotational speed, γ is bulk weight, and V is the material volume. For a single screw, the geometric volume is Vsingle = (π/4)h(d² − dw²); for a double screw, Vdouble = (π/2)h(d² − dw²). The corresponding efficiencies are ηsingle = 4D/[nγπh(d² − dw²)] and ηdouble = 2D/[nγπh(d² − dw²)]. Geometry and operating effects are expressed through helix angle tanϕ = πd/h, Froude number Fr = dπ²n²/g, and reactor incline β, giving η = f(β; tanϕ; Fr). The cited experiments fitted η = c0 exp(−c1Fr): short pitches/high helix angles produced approximately 60–80% efficiency, whereas longer pitches produced about 5–20%; one prototype reached roughly 90%. The excerpt assumes equivalent, non-interacting screws and identical granular material, ignores rolling coefficient effects, and describes full-fill/slip-free theory despite practical fill levels of 15–45%. It contains no quantitative experimental-versus-DEM errors, detailed material identification, Roberts–Willis slopes, Li et al. (2020), or Owen–Cleary methodology.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the nonlocal granular fluidity (NGF) formulation rather than providing the paper’s exact silo discharge-rate curves. The constitutive relation uses a fluidity field g, with diffusion proportional to A d²∇²g, so local flow depends on neighboring events and the mean grain size. The dimensionless nonlocal amplitude A is the principal additional steady-state material parameter; representative values are approximately 0.5 for glass beads and 0.9 for stiff DEM disks. Setting A=0 recovers inertial local μ(I) rheology. The excerpt motivates a grain-scale critical aperture by stating that silo jamming occurs when opening width competes with grain size, although it does not state a numerical critical aperture or a quantitative silo-experiment comparison. It reports quantitative validation against DEM stoppage data in other two-dimensional geometries and close agreement with glass-bead inclined-chute Hstop data. For silo implementation, NGF is augmented with a stress-free disconnected phase, identified by density ρ<ρc, while dense material is treated as plastically incompressible at ρ=ρc. The model uses Neumann fluidity conditions at free-surface and dense/disconnected interfaces, initializes newly reconsolidated material with g=0, and is implemented in an elasto-plastic/complex-Maxwell framework with an elastic spring whose stiffness vanishes below ρc. The excerpt does not contain exact flow-rate curves or their fitted experimental parameters.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes validation and implementation of the nonlocal granular-fluidity (NGF) model for wide inclined chutes, not the silo-clogging flow-rate results requested. It does not provide exact silo discharge-rate curves, a quantitative silo experiment comparison, or a grain-scale critical aperture. The local μ(I) model is used only during initialization: it generates a transient flow field and a nonzero granular-fluidity field g, after which g evolves under the NGF equation toward steady state. This is necessary because g = 0 is also an exact numerical solution and would otherwise remain unseeded. The simulations use a 2D plane-strain material-point method with one column of 1 mm elements, 16 material points per element, periodic left/right boundaries, no-slip at the bottom, and g Dirichlet/Neumann boundary conditions. Common parameters include grain diameter d = 5 mm, grain density ρs = 2450 kg m−3, gravity |G| = 9.81 m s−2, timestep Δt = 3 × 10−6 s, t0 = 1 ms, 10t0 initialization, and 20 s total simulation time. The code reproduces the analytical Hstop flow/no-flow boundary and limiting NGF velocity profiles. The only stated experimental comparison is with glass-bead chute data from Pouliquen (1999), while tall layers approach the local/Bagnold limit.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Dunatunga and Kamrin’s use of the dynamic Nonlocal Granular Fluidity (NGF) model to predict silo flow and clogging. Unlike local µ(I) rheology, which has no intrinsic length scale and generally predicts continued flow through a finite opening, NGF introduces a grain-size-dependent spatial diffusion of granular fluidity. Its key inputs include mean grain size d, solid density ρs, time scale t0, stress-ratio parameters µs and µ2, their difference Δµ, and the dimensionless nonlocal amplitude A; the model relates strain rate to fluidity through γ̇ = gµ. The silo implementation extends a trans-phase granular-flow solver and adds a free-separation criterion, producing full-field numerical solutions. The model predicts arrest when aperture size becomes comparable to a small multiple of the mean grain size, with an arch-shaped bridge, and predicts diffuse flow spreading for larger openings. The supplied pages do not provide exact silo flow-rate curves, numerical critical-aperture values, or a detailed quantitative point-by-point comparison with experiments. They state that the clogging threshold agrees with previous experimental studies and that the intended continuum comparison is the aperture where ensemble-averaged flow rate vanishes. Validation mentioned here is primarily against analytical inclined-chute results and checks of grid refinement, pressure, jammed-arch shape, and flowing velocity fields.

contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates FEM against Jenike, Enstad, and McLean critical-outlet-width estimates for cohesive powders. Critical width increases with hopper half-angle and wall friction because wall lift increases; internal friction and flow-function slope also matter, while predictions depend strongly on arch shape and flow mode. Jenike/McLean assumptions fit mass-flow hoppers but diverge as funnel flow develops. For experiments, inputs included hopper angle, internal/wall friction, flow-function slope, cohesion, and bulk density: polymer (519 Pa cohesion, 440 kg/m³) flowed at 18.5 cm versus 18 cm; SiC (175 Pa, 900 kg/m³) at 9.4 versus 8.8 cm. FEM was excellent for polymer but overpredicted SiC.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?

contexts.context: The study finds spreadability cannot be compared independently of powder, recoater type, and speed: ANOVA showed significant interactions affecting surface roughness \(S_a\). AlSi10Mg had the worst application behavior despite generally acceptable flowability; only FT4 specific energy indicated this. 316L performed best with a hopper recoater, while Alloy 718 performed similarly or better with blade/roller systems. GranuDrum cohesive index (CI) trends matched blade-recoater roughness versus speed, but absolute values differed and CI did not predict unknown powders or roller/hopper behavior. Laser scanning produced lower variance than digital microscopy; bed density was not measured.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates DEM models of single- and double-screw reactors at 0.75–12 Hz using Hertz contacts and material-specific restitution, friction, rolling friction, density, bulk density, particle radius, Young’s modulus, and geometry. Simulations used a 2×10⁻⁶ s timestep, 30,000–500,000 particles, and horizontal screws. Lower-pitch results closely followed experiments; transport efficiency was relatively stable, while steep pitches often predicted about 60% versus an expected 70%. Flight width, clearance, blade thickness, diameter, and pitch strongly affected theoretical volume and mass flow, especially in small screws. Biomass required much longer computation than steel spheres.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a limited but relevant finding for comparing flowability tests with powder-bed spreading. In the Cordova et al. study, moisturized powder flowability could be evaluated using applicator-based tools, whereas the Hall-flowmeter could not adequately test the moisturized material. Across the humidity conditions, the applicator tools did not show significant differences in measured flowability; however, the open applicator exhibited less variation between moisture states and was therefore recommended. This indicates that moisture-sensitive powders may produce different practical outcomes depending on the test method, and that a conventional Hall-flow result may fail to represent flow behavior under humidified conditions. The passage does not provide the requested ASTM-method-by-method comparison (Hall B213, Carney B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, shear/FT4, D7891, ring/D6773, drying, or moisture), nor does it report detailed AlSi10Mg correlations. It only supports the broader conclusion that conventional flowability measurements may not fully predict powder-bed spreadability, particularly when moisture changes cohesion and when the measurement tool does not reproduce the spreading process. The cited article concerns pre-treated and moisturized powders for laser powder bed fusion.
contexts.question: Using Gibbons review and Brocksieper and Cordova, which tests (ASTM Hall B213 Carney B964 B212 B527 B214 B822 shear FT4 D7891 ring D6773 drying moisture) measure what, and when do flowability and powder-bed spreadability correlate or fail? report practical comparison including AlSi10Mg.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a practical distinction between conventional flowability tests and tests intended to better represent powder-bed-fusion conditions. Angle of repose (AoR), obtainable with funnel methods such as Hall or Carney, is a simple cohesion/flowability indicator; values around 35° or less generally indicate lower cohesion and better flow. However, the review notes that no metal-PBF-specific standard exists for AoR. Rotating-drum testing measures dynamic avalanching behavior, including avalanche angle and flow regimes; rolling indicates the highest flowability, and drum speed can be selected to approximate recoater speeds. No publicly available standard is identified for this method. Shear testers (Jenike, Schulze, and Freeman) measure dynamic bulk behavior under defined stress conditions, while the Freeman FT4 rheometer is especially relevant to PBF because it evaluates low-stress dynamic flow. FT4 outputs include basic flow energy, flow rate, consolidation indices, conditioned bulk density, specific energy, and aerated energy; lower specific energy indicates better flowability. Automated rheometry improves repeatability but requires powder conditioning. These points help compare Hall/Carney, shear, ring-shear, and FT4 approaches, but the excerpt does not address ASTM methods B213, B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, D7891, D6773, drying/moisture, Brocksieper and Cordova, or AlSi10Mg-specific correlations between flowability and powder-bed spreadability.

contexts.context: This excerpt directly supports comparison of Hall flow time with powder-bed spreadability measured using open and funnel applicator tools, but it does not provide information on the specific ASTM tests listed in the question (Carney B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, shear/FT4, D7891, ring D6773, or drying-moisture protocols). Hall flow measures the time required for 50 g of powder to discharge; moisturized powders did not freely flow and therefore could not be assessed by this method. In contrast, the open and funnel tools assess deposited-layer relative density, which reflects both powder flowability and compaction within the tool. Correlation between flowability and spreadability is therefore not guaranteed. Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V flowed fastest, attributed partly to their higher density and regular, spherical morphology. AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy flowed more slowly as lightweight alloys; AlSi10Mg was particularly poor because of its irregular/coarser morphology and low shape factor (0.73), despite having a density close to Scalmalloy. Drying generally improved Hall flow slightly, while moisturizing tended to reduce relative density in spreadability tests. Vacuum drying produced more homogeneous results, whereas humidity, morphology, particle-wall interactions, and compaction affected repeatability and could make flowability results diverge from spreadability performance.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a general framework for comparing flowability tests with powder-bed spreadability, but it does not contain the requested ASTM-specific measurements or results from Gibbons’ review and Cordova. It identifies funnel tests (including Hall flow, Carney funnel, and Gustavsson funnel) as measuring the time required for a defined powder quantity to discharge; angle-of-repose testing as measuring the angle at which powder remains at rest; rotating-drum testing as measuring avalanche angle; ring-shear testing as measuring flowability under shear load; and powder-rheometer testing as measuring the energy required to move a rotating blade through powder. The study evaluates spreadability through global powder-bed surface roughness measured by laser scanning. It reports that links were found between spreadability and powder-rheometer/rotating-drum parameters, but emphasizes that relationships depend on powder properties, recoater type, and recoating speed. The roller recoater gave the lowest roughness across the investigated powders and speeds. The excerpt does not specify ASTM B213, B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, D7891, D6773, moisture-drying protocols, or AlSi10Mg-specific results, nor does it establish when correlations fail beyond noting system and parameter interactions.

contexts.context: This excerpt is a bibliography rather than the review’s explanatory discussion, so it provides only partial support for the requested practical comparison. It identifies standards and studies covering particle-size-related measurements (ASTM B330 air-permeability estimation of average particle size; ASTM B922 physical-adsorption specific surface area), particle-size reporting and analysis (ASTM E1617 and E2651), powder rheology and flow behavior, and bulk shear strength/cohesion (ASTM D6128 Jenike shear cell, ASTM D6773 Schulze ring shear tester, and ASTM D7891 FT4 powder-rheometer shear cell). It also cites Freeman’s comparative work on consolidated, conditioned, and aerated powders, plus literature specifically addressing powder rheology in additive manufacturing and the influence of particle-size distribution on powder-bed density, surface quality, and mechanical properties. The excerpt does not describe ASTM Hall flow (B213), Carney flow (B964), apparent density (B212), tap density (B527), flow-rate methods (B214), particle-size analysis (B822), drying/moisture procedures, or Brocksieper and Cordova. It likewise contains no evidence about when flowability correlates—or fails to correlate—with powder-bed spreadability, and no AlSi10Mg-specific comparison. Those conclusions require the omitted body text or the cited source papers.

contexts.context: Brocksieper et al. show that conventional flowability measurements cannot be treated as universal predictors of powder-bed spreadability. Spreadability, assessed primarily through powder-layer arithmetic mean roughness (Sa), depends strongly on interactions among powder, recoater type, and recoating speed. AlSi10Mg had the worst application behavior with every recoater, despite this not being apparent from most flowability tests; among the reported parameters, only the FT4 specific energy (SE) identified its poorest flow behavior. The study found no relationship between rotating-cylinder avalanche angle (AA) or dynamic angle (DA) and observed application behavior. GranuDrum cohesive index (CI) tracked Sa trends for the blade recoater and could therefore extrapolate the behavior of a known powder at other blade-recoating speeds, but it could not predict an unknown powder’s spreading behavior. Roller and hopper recoaters behaved differently. The excerpt does not describe ASTM Hall, Carney, B213, B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, shear, D7891 ring, D6773, drying, or moisture tests, nor does it provide the Gibbons review or Cordova comparison. Thus, those tests’ measured quantities and cross-study practical correlations must be supplied from the other sources; this excerpt mainly supports treating flowability–spreadability correlations as powder- and process-specific.
contexts.question: Using Gibbons review and Brocksieper and Cordova, which tests (ASTM Hall B213 Carney B964 B212 B527 B214 B822 shear FT4 D7891 ring D6773 drying moisture) measure what, and when do flowability and powder-bed spreadability correlate or fail? report practical comparison including AlSi10Mg.

contexts.context: This excerpt establishes the practical distinction between conventional powder-flow tests and L-PBF powder-bed spreadability. It states that flowability is important for layer continuity, uniformity, apparent density, and repeatability, but cautions that available flowability techniques may not accurately represent the thin-layer spreading mechanism. Cordova et al. therefore developed two applicator tools specifically for measuring spreadability in thin-layer application and compared results with standard characterization, including morphology, moisture content, chemical composition, and Hall-flowmeter flowability. The relevant material variables are particle morphology, particle-size distribution, surface topology, friction, mechanical interlocking, interparticle forces, and liquid bridging. The excerpt particularly supports a moisture-sensitive comparison: among Inconel 718, Ti6Al4V, AlSi10Mg, and Scalmalloy, AlSi10Mg was most susceptible to moisture and oxygen uptake, with substantial reductions in spreadability and relative density on the build platform. It also notes that direct measurement of moisture in metal powders is challenging. Thus, conventional flowability values should not automatically be treated as direct predictors of spreading performance; correlation can depend on powder morphology, environmental conditioning, and alloy-specific moisture response. The excerpt does not provide the requested ASTM/ISO test-by-test results or numerical correlations for Hall, Carney, B213, B964, B212, B527, B214, B822, FT4, D7891, ring shear, D6773, drying, or moisture methods.

contexts.context: This excerpt is primarily the reference list from Gibbons et al.’s review and does not provide the requested test-by-test definitions or direct results for Brocksieper and Cordova. It does, however, identify the relevant evidence base. ASTM B527 is explicitly cited as a tap-density method, while Abdullah and Geldart are cited regarding bulk-density measurements as flowability indicators. The bibliography also points to Hall-flow and Arnold-density evaluation, flow-rate studies, angle-of-repose testing, and broader reviews of powder-flow testers and characterization methods. For powder-bed behavior, the cited literature distinguishes conventional flowability from spreading or layer quality: Jacob et al. investigate particle-size-distribution effects on powder-bed density; Le et al. examine powder-layer quality as a function of feedstock and recoating; Hulme-Smith et al. address spreadability testing; and Mitterlehner et al. propose a problem-oriented spreadability device and routine. Brika et al. specifically connect morphology and size distribution with flowability and laser powder-bed-fusion manufacturability, although their alloy is Ti-6Al-4V rather than AlSi10Mg. Thus, this excerpt supports comparing flowability tests with spreadability/recoating tests, but it does not contain enough information to state what ASTM B213, Carney, B964, B212, B214, B822, FT4, D7891, ring shear, D6773, or drying/moisture tests measure, nor to establish AlSi10Mg-specific correlations or failures.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes powder characterization relevant to flowability and PBF spreadability. Optical/SEM/TEM microscopy can detect contamination, agglomeration, discoloration from thermal exposure, attrition, and particle damage caused by recoating, mixing, or recovery. SEM-EDS enables elemental contamination mapping; XRD examines crystal structure. Morphology strongly affects flowability and bulk density. ASTM F1877 and ISO 9276-6 define measurements such as Feret/Martin/project-area diameters, aspect ratio, elongation, roundness, equivalent-circle diameter, and form factor; ImageJ supports analysis. Skeletal density and internal porosity can be measured by gas pycnometry, CT, permeability, or adsorption, influencing PBF porosity.
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that powder morphology and bulk properties strongly affect flow and PBF performance. Sphericity, irregularity, and PSD (reported as D10, D50, D90; ASTM E1617/E2651) influence packing density, while smaller particles can fill voids. Gas permeability estimates bulk density, particle size, and specific surface area; adsorption (ASTM B922) measures accessible surface area. AFM/nanoindentation provide modulus, hardness, yield stress, toughness, adhesion, and friction. Tap density (ASTM B527) reflects rearrangement and air-gap reduction, while Hall/Carney funnel tests measure flow rate and angle of repose; flow depends strongly on particle size and cohesiveness.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents Heterarchical Granular Dynamics (HGD), a stochastic framework bridging particle and continuum models through void migration, multiscale heterarchical physics, and stress calculations. It represents arbitrarily many grains and captures flowing/stable states, segregation, mixing, and stress distributions. Validation used X-ray radiography of Jasmine-rice discharge through a 10-mm slit, granular-column collapse, and basal vertical-stress measurements; code is openly available at GitHub. HGD conserves mass, but currently omits momentum/energy conservation, inertia, particle breakage, and compaction. Its stochastic advection preserves mean motion, \(E[X(t)]=ut\), while diffusion gives \(Var(X(t))=2Dt\).

contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?

contexts.context: Particle-size distribution (PSD) can be measured statically (microscopy/CT with image analysis) or dynamically (light scattering), but laser diffraction assumes spherical particles, so sphericity must be verified. ASTM B243 defines bulk density as mass per volume including voids; ASTM B212 measures apparent density (AD) using a standard funnel and cup. Powder-bed density depends strongly on preparation. Flow-rate testing measures time for a standard mass/volume (typically 50 g) through Hall or Carney funnels; faster flow generally indicates lower cohesion. “Does not Flow” reflects high cohesion and poor repeatability; Scott or Arnold meters can then determine AD.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns a lattice/cellular model rather than auger discharge. Random movement intervals produce numerical dispersion: with timestep \(\Delta t\), mean interval \(T\Delta t\), \(\mathrm{Var}[X(t)]=u^2t\Delta tT\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{adv}}=u\sqrt{t\Delta tT}\). Diffusion follows \(\mathrm{Var}[X(t)]=2Dt\), with individual displacement variance \(2D\Delta t_i\). Slope-stability discretization depends on cell count \(M\); \(M\gtrsim60\) keeps angular error below \(1^\circ\). Additional appendices formulate size-dependent segregation and porosity/void transport using advection–diffusion equations and a Gaussian plume model.

snippets: Discrete modelling is impractical for industrial scales owing to the computational complexity.
Therefore, continuum modelling is often used for describing a granular flow at a large scale.
A frictional visco-plastic model called μ(I) rheology has been proposed, which provides quantitative descriptions of dense granular flows in different geometries.
The two key parameters that determine the regime criterion of granular flow and are included in all the proposed continuum models are the solid fraction and velocity (shear).
among all the flow configurations, hoppers are the most common ones in industrial applications.
The discharge rate and residence time distribution in the hopper ... are also determined by the solid fraction and the velocity of the particles.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents a 2D plane-strain material-point-method (MPM) silo implementation using nonlocal granular rheology (NGF), rather than providing information about Taichi MPM/ChainQueen, Uintah MPM, PySPH, OpenFOAM, Basilisk, or HGD. It specifies a fixed silo geometry and orifice width, varied grain diameter and nonlocal amplitude, and common parameters including E, ν, μs, μ2, density, relaxation time, and b = Δμ/I0. The authors use a large μ2 = 50; above approximately μ2 ∼ 10, results become insensitive to μ2, effectively producing a linear μ(I) local-limit fit. The model is initialized with lithostatic pressure and a short local-model run, after which the nonlocal procedure determines whether flow decays to a jammed g = 0 state or reaches a steady flowing state. The excerpt explains that a plane-strain jammed arch requires μ = 1, motivating μ2 ≥ 1, and notes the weaker fully three-dimensional constraint μ2 > √3/2. It does not explicitly confirm open-source code for any named software, discuss SPH continuum parcels versus actual grains, or report measured silo/screw mass-flow accuracy or comparisons with experiments. It also does not establish that the presented implementation itself is publicly released.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a stochastic “Heterarchical Granular Dynamics” model validated against granular-pile behavior. It reproduces angle of repose from \(0^\circ\)–\(90^\circ\), compaction toward a critical solid fraction \(\nu_c\), dilation of initially denser material, and bidisperse/polydisperse segregation (using a truncated power-law size distribution, Eq. 25). Predicted stress fields increase with depth and match sand experiments favorably. During silo discharge, void-plume width scales as \(\sqrt{2\alpha\bar{s}y}\), enabling calibration of \(\alpha\); comparison with rice X-ray data yielded \(\alpha\approx0.91\).
contexts.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which continuum and reduced-order physics models predict granular discharge through small orifices and screw conveyors for cohesive powders: Beverloo and modified Beverloo laws with cohesion, Jenike-Johanson arching and hopper design from shear-cell flow functions, Janssen stress saturation, mu(I) and non-local rheologies, Drucker-Prager or Mohr-Coulomb plasticity in FEM, the material point method, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, cellular automata and avalanche models, and screw-conveyor volumetric-efficiency models (for example Roberts; Owen and Cleary)? Which have open-source implementations (for example Taichi MPM, PySPH, Uintah, Basilisk, OpenFOAM granular solvers), what inputs do they need, and how accurately do they predict mass flow rate compared with DEM and experiment?

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates differentiable MPM, emphasizing numerical reliability rather than powder-flow laws. Deterministic fixed-point reductions produced bit-identical states/losses across five repeated f32/f64 configurations; ordinary GPU summation could even reverse a Poisson-ratio gradient’s sign. Finite-difference checks were reliable only for short rollouts: f64 AD/FD discrepancy was ≤1.5×10⁻⁵ at two steps and <3×10⁻⁵ at five/ten, but rose to 0.341 and 0.270 at 20/40 steps. Longer horizons increased validation cost (25–178 s). Objective choice mattered: PRT-CD descended in 97.5% of epochs, yet PRT-EMD achieved lower independent HMD (3698.6 vs 3738.4 mm).

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates Mohr–Coulomb FEM against Jenike, Enstad, and McLean critical-outlet-width theories. FEM predictions generally followed expected increases with internal friction angle and flow-function slope, but localized yielding caused deviations above \(\phi\approx40^\circ\). Linear flow-function FEM overpredicted fine SiC arching width (experiment 5 cm; FEM 10.4 cm), while a bilinear function reducing zero-stress yield strength by 50% improved predictions to 5.5–6.1 cm (10–21% error). Fine polymer predictions improved from 30 cm to 18–18.5 cm versus 20 cm measured. Accurate low-stress characterization (<~1000 Pa) is crucial; FEM handles complex geometries and nonlinear material behavior.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates differentiable MPM for elastoplastic and granular robotic manipulation, using fixed-corotated/von Mises and Hencky–Saint Venant/Drucker–Prager models. MPM transfers material between particles and a grid, but GPU many-to-one reductions introduce order-dependent rounding that contaminates long-horizon gradients. In a 311-step granular case, the GPU mean for ∂L/∂ν was **+1.29**, versus a deterministic CPU reference of **−7.99**, reversing the optimization direction. Initial discrepancies were approximately **10⁻⁷ (float32)** and **10⁻¹⁶ (float64)**. The authors recommend reproducible accumulation, finite-difference checks against repeated-run variation, and explicit objective reporting.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports distinguishing funnel flow, density, sieving/particle-size, rheometry, and shear testing, but it does not provide the requested ASTM designation-to-test mapping in full. It explicitly discusses Hall and Carney funnels as methods for determining angle of repose (AoR), while also noting that ISO 4324 addresses AoR for powders and granules and that no dedicated standard method exists for metal-powder PBF AoR. The passage identifies Jenike, Schulze, and Freeman instruments as common shear testers. Freeman FT4 rheometry is particularly relevant to PBF because it measures dynamic flow at low powder stresses and can provide basic flow energy, flow rate, consolidation indices, conditioned bulk density, specific energy, and aerated energy. Lower specific energy indicates better flowability, and conditioning is needed to reduce stress history and improve repeatability. contexts.context: This excerpt provides background for interpreting shear-flow testing, but it does not identify or map the requested ASTM standards, nor does it discuss a 3 mm micro-auger comparison or explicitly flag any standard misidentification. It explains that bulk flow depends on resistance to shear and that powder strength varies with the internal forces and stress state. For loosely consolidated material, initial shear strength may be low, then increase with continued deformation toward a critical-state value. Consequently, a shear-flow-function result obtained at low consolidation should be interpreted as a condition-specific measure rather than an intrinsic, fixed material property. Removing the compaction force and applying a lower normal load can reduce the initial shear resistance as the shear plane expands to the relevant yield strength. The excerpt also emphasizes that the preparation and loading history must match the intended storage or flow condition: Jenike testing relates consolidation load and normal load for shearing without volume change, while annular testing reaches steady state through continuous shearing. Permeability, trapped or moving void gas, moisture, density, and consolidation can materially alter measured strength. These points are relevant when comparing laboratory shear results with a small 3 mm auger, because the auger may impose different confinement, stress history, shear rate, and air/moisture conditions; however, the excerpt supplies no direct auger methodology or standard crosswalk.
